ela.mp3: I am 63. There is a song from a wedding in 1982. It was not my wedding. I danced with a man I never saw again. Every time it plays, I am 20 again for three minutes. Then it stops and I am 63, and that is fine.
ele.mp3: I train with the same song every morning. Not because I love it. I do not love it. It has 140 beats and my legs like that number. It makes me run 4 minutes longer. My girlfriend hates it. I do not care.
lab.mp3: 62 students listened to hits from 1955 to 2009. They knew the songs from their own 20s. That was expected. Then a second peak appeared and nobody expected it. The music their parents were young with. Years these students never lived. Some of your songs are not yours. You got them from somebody.
voz1.mp3: There is one song from my first job. The bass starts and my shoulders move before I decide. It makes me walk faster. I put it on when the kitchen is a mess. 20 minutes later, the kitchen is clean. It does not make me happy exactly. It makes me move.
voz2.mp3: My song is very slow. Piano and a woman singing in a language I do not speak. I do not know what the words mean. It makes me feel calm and a little sad at the same time. My wife says it makes me quiet. She is right. I play it in the car, alone.
voz3.mp3: This one is not my music. My father played it every Sunday morning. He sang it badly, in the kitchen, with the window open. Now I am 24 and I live far away. When it starts it reminds me of that kitchen, not of him, of the kitchen. That is strange, right?
voz4.mp3: There is a song I cannot listen to anymore. It was on in the car on a very bad day 10 years ago. Nothing is wrong with the song. It is a good song, but it makes me feel that day again. So I skip it. 10 seconds is enough.
